full_text_en:
Swiss Newco Commodities AG v. China Construction Bank, Hunchun City Sub-Branch, Jilin Province
— Appeal concerning refusal to pay under a letter of credit

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Swiss Newco Commodities AG (NEWCO COMMODITIES AG), domiciled at Utere Allmendstrasse 11, CH-6312 Steinhausen/Zug, Switzerland

Legal Representative: Othmar Jung, President

Agent ad litem: Xie Chaohua and Gao Kuanzhong, attorneys from Beijing Xie Chaohua Law Firm

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): China Construction Bank, Hunchun City Sub-Branch, Jilin Province, domiciled at Yinhe Building, South Street, Hunchun City, Jilin Province, People’s Republic of China

Person in Charge: Chen Chengnan, Branch Manager

Agent ad litem: Du Qingchun and Duan Donghui, officers of the Legal Advisory Office of China Construction Bank

The Appellant, Swiss Newco Commodities AG (hereinafter “Newco”), appealed against the civil judgment (1997) Ji Jing Chu Zi No. 100 of the Jilin Provincial High People’s Court of the People’s Republic of China in its action against the Respondent, China Construction Bank, Hunchun City Sub-Branch, Jilin Province (hereinafter “CCB Hunchun”), concerning the refusal to pay the proceeds under a letter of credit, and appealed to the Supreme People’s Court of the People’s Republic of China.

Facts Found by the Supreme People’s Court

On November 6, 1995, the Respondent, CCB Hunchun, issued an irrevocable documentary letter of credit No. JLHCLC95302 in the amount of USD 1,460,000. The applicant was Jilin Province Foreign Trade Import and Export Corporation (hereinafter “Jilin Foreign Trade”), the beneficiary was the Appellant, Newco, and the advising bank was the Frankfurt Branch of Bank of New York (hereinafter “Frankfurt Branch”). The letter of credit stated that it was subject to the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits, International Chamber of Commerce Publication No. 500 (1993 Revision) (hereinafter “UCP500”).

On November 18 of the same year, Newco began shipping the goods under the letter of credit. On December 5 of the same year, Newco presented the documents under the letter of credit to the Frankfurt Branch and requested payment. After examining the documents, the Frankfurt Branch, on December 8 of the same year, sent a telex to CCB Hunchun, pointing out seven discrepancies: (1) The railway consignment note was issued in Russian; (2) Two railway consignment notes numbered 50332 and 50331 were missing; (3) Delay in shipment; (4) The railway and carriage numbers on the packing list did not match those on the railway consignment notes; (5) The contract number on the invoice did not match other documents; (6) Point 2 in the quality certificate did not conform to the letter of credit and invoice; (7) The packaging method in the beneficiary’s fax did not conform to the letter of credit, and the shipment date was incorrect, etc. The Frankfurt Branch requested CCB Hunchun to instruct whether to accept the documents.

On December 15 of the same year, CCB Hunchun sent a telex to the Frankfurt Branch, clearly stating refusal to pay. Due to a telecommunications equipment malfunction, the telex was illegible, and the Frankfurt Branch asked CCB Hunchun to resend it. On December 18, CCB Hunchun resent the telex. Subsequently, the Frankfurt Branch notified Newco of CCB Hunchun’s telex refusing payment and returned the entire set of documents under the letter of credit to Newco. During this period, the goods shipped by Newco were taken by Hunchun City Guomao Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “Hunchun Guomao”), which had a foreign trade agency relationship with Jilin Foreign Trade. Newco, having failed to recover the proceeds from CCB Hunchun, filed a lawsuit with the Jilin Provincial High People’s Court of the People’s Republic of China, requesting a judgment ordering CCB Hunchun to pay the proceeds under the letter of credit plus interest and compensate for its losses.

Further investigation revealed that the letter of credit No. JLHCLC95302 was applied for by Hunchun Guomao in the name of Jilin Foreign Trade based on the foreign trade agency agreement between Hunchun Guomao and Jilin Foreign Trade.

The above facts are confirmed by the letter of credit No. JLHCLC95302, the relevant documents, and the exchanged telexes.

Opinion of the Court of First Instance

(1) After the letter of credit issued by CCB Hunchun was advised by the Frankfurt Branch and accepted by Newco, the letter of credit took legal effect and created binding obligations among the parties to the letter of credit. Newco knew that Jilin Foreign Trade was not the buyer under the international sales contract but accepted a letter of credit with Jilin Foreign Trade as the applicant, indicating that in this letter of credit transaction, Newco valued CCB Hunchun’s primary liability for payment. The conduct of the non-party Hunchun Guomao, which used an agency agreement in place of a letter of credit application and applied for the letter of credit in the name of Jilin Foreign Trade, violated the general procedure for issuing letters of credit. CCB Hunchun, as the issuing bank, was somewhat at fault for failing to scrutinize this properly.

(2) In this case, the Frankfurt Branch acted both as the advising bank and the negotiating bank. When it delivered the letter of credit to Newco, it was acting as the advising bank, and its relationship with CCB Hunchun was one of principal and agent. Once the Frankfurt Branch accepted CCB Hunchun’s designation and became the negotiating bank, a relationship between the holder and the drawee under negotiable instruments law was formed between it and CCB Hunchun. Only after the negotiating bank obtained qualified documents and negotiated them with the beneficiary did it have the right to hold the documents and request the issuing bank to pay the proceeds under the letter of credit. The Frankfurt Branch’s examination of documents as the negotiating bank was for the purpose of confirming whether the documents presented by Newco were qualified. The branch telexed the seven discrepancies found during its document examination to CCB Hunchun to first obtain instructions from CCB Hunchun before negotiating with the beneficiary, thereby increasing the insurance factor for itself when later presenting the documents to the issuing bank for payment. This did not constitute document examination on behalf of the issuing bank. After receiving the documents from the negotiating bank, the issuing bank still had the right to examine them and could refuse payment if discrepancies were found. CCB Hunchun, as the issuing bank, and the Frankfurt Branch, as the negotiating bank, each had independent rights to examine documents and bore responsibility for the consequences of their own examinations. The seven banking-day periods specified in UCP500 Articles 13(b) and 14(d) for the issuing bank to examine documents and reject them both commence from the banking day following the issuing bank’s receipt of the documents. Only upon receipt of the documents is the issuing bank bound by the seven banking-day period. CCB Hunchun expressed its refusal to pay under the letter of credit after receiving the telex from the Frankfurt Branch. From the issuance of the letter of credit until the refusal to pay, CCB Hunchun never received any documents from the Frankfurt Branch or Newco and never exercised its right to examine documents. Therefore, its expression of refusal was not subject to the seven banking-day limitation. Newco’s argument that the negotiating bank’s document examination represented that of the issuing bank and that their relationship should be governed by the agency provisions of the General Principles of Civil Law was untenable.

(3) Letter of credit transactions are documentary transactions, and at all stages of the letter of credit, the principle of strict compliance must be observed. The principle that documents must conform to each other and to the terms of the credit has been adopted by banks in various countries and recognized by the International Chamber of Commerce. Based on this principle, the seven discrepancies mentioned in the telex of the Frankfurt Branch were factually supported. Newco’s argument that those seven discrepancies were not established could not be accepted.

(4) Although CCB Hunchun was at fault in the process of issuing the letter of credit, this did not constitute collusion with the non-party to defraud Newco and did not affect the validity of the letter of credit it issued. Newco’s assertion during the trial that CCB Hunchun had colluded with the non-party to commit fraud lacked sufficient evidence and was not supported. The issue of Newco’s goods being taken by another party without payment could be pursued separately through other means of resolving commercial disputes.

Accordingly, the court rendered the following judgment: Newco’s claims were dismissed. The case acceptance fee of RMB 81,040 was borne by Newco.

Grounds of Appeal

Newco, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed, arguing: The Respondent, CCB Hunchun, knowing that Hunchun Guomao applied for the letter of credit in the name of Jilin Foreign Trade, issued the letter of credit, which constituted collusion with Hunchun Guomao to use the letter of credit for fraud and to obtain its goods; CCB Hunchun’s conduct, including exceeding the document examination period, violated the provisions of UCP500, and CCB Hunchun had no right to refuse payment and should bear the obligation to pay; the first-instance judgment erred in fact-finding and misapplied the law, and requested that the judgment be amended to order CCB Hunchun to compensate the Appellant, Newco, for its loss of proceeds and interest.

Respondent’s Defense

CCB Hunchun argued: Hunchun Guomao’s application for the letter of credit in the name of Jilin Foreign Trade did not affect the validity of the letter of credit; the Appellant Newco’s claim that the Respondent CCB Hunchun conspired with Hunchun Guomao to commit fraud was unfounded; CCB Hunchun’s refusal to pay under the letter of credit due to discrepancies complied with the provisions of UCP500; the first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly and should be affirmed.

Opinion of the Supreme People’s Court

This case concerns a dispute over the refusal to pay proceeds under a letter of credit between the beneficiary and the issuing bank. Both parties agreed that the letter of credit in this case was subject to UCP500, and this agreement is valid. Therefore, the rights and obligations of the parties should be adjusted in accordance with this uniform practice. The letter of credit transaction is a legal relationship with independence. After the Appellant, Newco, accepted the letter of credit issued by the Respondent, CCB Hunchun, CCB Hunchun assumed an independent primary obligation to pay, unrelated to the applicant. Newco’s claim that CCB Hunchun colluded with Hunchun Guomao to use the letter of credit for fraud and to obtain the goods under the letter of credit lacked any factual basis and was also inconsistent with legal principles.

According to UCP500, the issuing bank has a period of seven banking days from the banking day following its receipt of the documents to examine them. However, in this case, the issuing bank, CCB Hunchun, never received the documents under the letter of credit from the outset. After learning that the Frankfurt Branch had telexed discrepancies, CCB Hunchun sent a telex without delay, which did not violate the provisions of UCP500. Newco’s ground of appeal that CCB Hunchun exceeded the document examination period was untenable.

In a letter of credit relationship, the issuing bank has a strict duty to examine documents and determines whether to pay based on whether the documents appear on their face to comply with the terms and conditions of the credit. Payment under the letter of credit can only be made when the documents are in compliance with each other and with the terms of the credit. In this case, the documents submitted by Newco contained numerous material discrepancies, and CCB Hunchun’s refusal to pay under the letter of credit on that basis was proper.

The fact that Newco’s goods were taken by Hunchun Guomao without payment being received has nothing to do with CCB Hunchun and does not fall within the scope of this case. Newco should pursue this matter through other avenues. Newco’s grounds of appeal were not sustainable and were not supported.

The first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly and should be affirmed.

Accordingly, the Supreme People’s Court, pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Subparagraph (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on March 6, 1999:

Judgment

The appeal is dismissed, and the first-instance judgment is affirmed.

The case acceptance fee for the first instance shall be borne as determined by the first-instance judgment. The case acceptance fee for the second instance, RMB 81,040, shall be borne by the Appellant, Swiss Newco Commodities AG.
